top_level_objectives: Understand the three-dimensional structure of the DNA double helix and identify its key components (sugar-phosphate backbones, nitrogenous bases, hydrogen bonds)
Explain the antiparallel orientation of DNA strands and the directional nature of the sugar-phosphate backbone (5' to 3' polarity)
Visualize and describe the complementary base-pairing rules and their hydrogen bonding patterns
Trace the semiconservative replication process including the roles of helicase, single-strand binding proteins, DNA polymerase, and DNA ligase
Explain why leading and lagging strand synthesis occur asymmetrically and how Okazaki fragments relate to the antiparallel structure
Demonstrate how semiconservative replication produces daughter DNA molecules, each containing one parental and one new strand

scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce the overall 3D structure of the DNA molecule and orient students to its key geometric features.
key_visuals: A large, rotating DNA double helix model in the center of the workspace showing the full helical shape
Two clearly colored sugar-phosphate backbones (e.g., one blue, one orange) spiraling around a central axis
Nitrogenous bases projecting inward in contrasting colors
Labels indicating the major and minor grooves
student_actions: Rotate the helix freely to examine it from multiple angles
Toggle visibility of individual components (backbones, bases, grooves) to isolate them
Observe the spiral geometry and symmetry of the structure

scenes.brief_purpose: Establish the directionality of DNA strands and explain how antiparallel orientation emerges from 5' to 3' polarity.
key_visuals: One DNA strand isolated and enlarged, showing the sugar-phosphate backbone with numbered carbon atoms in the deoxyribose rings
Clear visual distinction between 5' and 3' ends using color or textured markers
An arrow overlay or animation showing the 5' to 3' direction along one strand
A second complementary strand oriented oppositely, with arrows showing its 3' to 5' direction
student_actions: Identify the 5' and 3' ends of one strand
Trace the sugar-phosphate backbone by tapping or selecting sequential nucleotides
Recognize that the second strand runs in the opposite direction and explain why this is antiparallel
Answer a prompt or toggle visibility to confirm understanding of directionality

scenes.brief_purpose: Visualize the complementary base-pairing rules and the different numbers of hydrogen bonds between A-T and G-C pairs.
key_visuals: A zoomed-in, cross-section view of several base pairs within the helix
Two opposing bases colored and labeled (e.g., adenine in red, thymine in blue)
White, dotted lines representing hydrogen bonds between the pair
A second pair (guanine and cytosine) showing three hydrogen bonds instead of two
Annotations or counts showing 2 H-bonds for A-T and 3 H-bonds for G-C
student_actions: Identify which bases pair together by selecting them
Count the hydrogen bonds visually for both A-T and G-C pairs
Predict complementary strand sequences given a parental strand sequence by selecting or placing bases
Confirm predictions reveal the correct pairing through color-change or lock-in feedback

scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce the start of replication by showing how helicase unwinds the double helix at the replication fork.
key_visuals: A DNA double helix with a replication fork at one end, partially unwound
A helicase enzyme (protein complex) positioned at the fork, breaking hydrogen bonds between base pairs
The two parental strands separating and moving apart
Single-strand binding proteins (SSBs) coating the exposed single strands to prevent re-annealing
Color-coded strands (e.g., parental strands in a distinct hue, newly synthesized in another)
student_actions: Play an animation showing helicase moving along the helix and unwinding it
Tap on the helicase molecule to see information about its function
Observe as SSBs bind to single strands and stabilize them
Drag or move the helicase along the DNA to continue unwinding (optional simulation)

scenes.brief_purpose: Show how DNA polymerase synthesizes the leading strand continuously in the 5' to 3' direction, following the replication fork.
key_visuals: The replication fork with the leading strand template (running 3' to 5' toward the fork)
DNA polymerase enzyme positioned on the template, adding nucleotides
The newly synthesized leading strand growing continuously and unidirectionally
Directional arrows showing 5' to 3' synthesis direction
Incoming nucleotides (dNTPs) and the release of pyrophosphate during polymerization
student_actions: Observe the continuous synthesis of the leading strand as the fork progresses
Identify the template strand and the direction of synthesis
Drag incoming nucleotides to match base pairs (guided interaction)
Confirm that synthesis proceeds uninterrupted in one direction

scenes.scene_name: Lagging Strand Synthesis and Okazaki Fragments
scenes.brief_purpose: Explain why the lagging strand must be synthesized discontinuously in short fragments (Okazaki fragments) because the template runs toward the fork.
key_visuals: The lagging strand template running 5' to 3' toward the replication fork
Multiple DNA polymerase molecules positioned at intervals on the lagging template
Okazaki fragments being synthesized discontinuously in the 5' to 3' direction, moving away from the fork
Each fragment growing independently until the next polymerase reaches it
RNA primers (short RNA sequences) at the 5' end of each fragment, shown in a distinct color
student_actions: Identify why the lagging strand template's orientation forces discontinuous synthesis
Observe multiple polymerase molecules working simultaneously on different fragments
Count or note the approximate length of Okazaki fragments
Predict the direction of synthesis on the lagging strand (5' to 3' even though fragments grow away from the fork)

scenes.brief_purpose: Show how DNA ligase seals the nicks between Okazaki fragments to complete the new lagging strand.
key_visuals: Several Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand, each with gaps (nicks) between them where the 3' end of one fragment meets the 5' end of the next
RNA primers still visible at the start of each fragment
DNA ligase enzyme approaching and binding to each nick
The phosphodiester bond forming as the ligase catalyzes the sealing of the nick
Completed, continuous lagging strand after all ligations
student_actions: Identify the location of nicks between Okazaki fragments
Observe or simulate DNA ligase binding and sealing nicks
Tap on each joining site to confirm the phosphodiester bond formation
Compare the leading and lagging strands after synthesis is complete

scenes.brief_purpose: Demonstrate that each daughter DNA molecule contains one original parental strand and one newly synthesized strand, validating the semiconservative model.
key_visuals: Two complete daughter DNA molecules displayed side-by-side, clearly labeled
One parental strand in each daughter colored distinctly (e.g., dark blue) to show it was inherited from the original helix
One newly synthesized strand in each daughter in a contrasting color (e.g., light blue or green)
A visual trace or highlighting showing which parental strand went to which daughter
A summary label showing each daughter as having 50% parental and 50% new DNA
student_actions: Identify which strand in each daughter molecule is the original parental strand
Confirm that no daughter molecule contains two fully new strands or two parental strands
Rotate and examine both daughter molecules to verify they are identical in sequence
Answer a reflection question about why this is called semiconservative replication and how it differs from conservative or dispersive models
